findings.name: detection-misses-2026-10-05.md
findings.title: Why OWLv2 missed what it missed: detector or prompt? (sim, 5 Oct 2026)
findings.excerpt:
**Mostly the prompt, and a little the threshold. Not the detector.** No miss is an in-view toy of ordinary size that
OWLv2 cannot see:

- **The bowl and the dinosaurs** sit outside the 12 prompts' words. They score 0.06 to 0.19 with them, and 0.35 to
  0.60 when asked about with "small object" or "object on the floor". This is a prompt failure.
- **The lion, the other dinosaur and the lacing sheep** are seen, but just under the line: 0.09 to 0.19, against
  thresholds of 0.15 and 0.2.
- **The 1×1 Lego brick** is 2 to 6 pixels across. It is too small for base at this resolution. Large, with its finer
  patches, does pick it up in one house.
- **House 96's card game** never comes within the 2.5 m range in which the arm places detections. Large's miss of it
  is a matter of where the camera went, not of recognition. Base's "find" of it was a coincidence: its box was on the
  lacing sheep, which lies within reach of both toys.

Adding one generic prompt, "small object", to the 12 finds 3 more toys for each model on these nights. It costs no
extra false positives and loses no toy that was found before. That figure is fitted to these nights (below).
findings.full:
> **Why this is here:** a short, clean diagnosis of a question every open-vocabulary detector raises: when it misses,
> is it the model or the words it was given? Here it was mostly the words (detection-baselines [XEi], [En1]).

The question: when the detector fails to detect a toy, is that a failure of the detector or of the prompt? This
diagnoses every toy that OWLv2 base and OWLv2 large missed as detectors in
the recognizers round of 4 Oct (detection-baselines [80w]'s Tests row), on its 270 frames and 48 toys, with the 12 prompts of [XEi] ([En1]'s
recognizers). Sim only; everything ran on the laptop; nothing was sent to any hosted service. This is a **diagnosis,
not a result**. It reads the truth, and the generic-prompt thresholds were matched using all six nights' truth.

## Answer

**Mostly the prompt, and a little the threshold. Not the detector.** No miss is an in-view toy of ordinary size that
OWLv2 cannot see:

- **The bowl and the dinosaurs** sit outside the 12 prompts' words. They score 0.06 to 0.19 with them, and 0.35 to
  0.60 when asked about with "small object" or "object on the floor". This is a prompt failure.
- **The lion, the other dinosaur and the lacing sheep** are seen, but just under the line: 0.09 to 0.19, against
  thresholds of 0.15 and 0.2.
- **The 1×1 Lego brick** is 2 to 6 pixels across. It is too small for base at this resolution. Large, with its finer
  patches, does pick it up in one house.
- **House 96's card game** never comes within the 2.5 m range in which the arm places detections. Large's miss of it
  is a matter of where the camera went, not of recognition. Base's "find" of it was a coincidence: its box was on the
  lacing sheep, which lies within reach of both toys.

Adding one generic prompt, "small object", to the 12 finds 3 more toys for each model on these nights. It costs no
extra false positives and loses no toy that was found before. That figure is fitted to these nights (below).

## Counts

| Class | OWLv2 base (thr 0.2): 7 misses | OWLv2 large (thr 0.15): 6 misses |
|---|---|---|
| threshold (best score on the toy at least half the threshold) | **2**: s76 lion (0.149), s76 dinosaur dino_5 (0.191) | **3**: s71 dinosaur dino_5 (0.126), s76 bowl (0.090), s96 lacing sheep (0.088) |
| prompt, generic (12 + a generic prompt finds it at the original false-positive level) | **3**: s71 bowl, s76 bowl, s71 dinosaur | **1**: s71 bowl |
| prompt, specific (only its own name finds it) | 0 | 0 |
| resolution/size (projected long side under 20 px) | **2**: s71 Lego 1×1 (6 px), s76 Lego 1×1 (3 px) | **1**: s76 Lego 1×1 (3 px) |
| detector (nothing finds it, and it is large enough) | 0 | 0 |
| not in view (no frame sees it within the arm's 2.5 m placement range; a class added below) | 0 | **1**: s96 card game |

The classes overlap. The first that holds is given, in the order of the table. Of the threshold class:

- For base, the lion is also found by its own name ("lion", 0.277). The s76 dinosaur is also found by "small object"
  at the matched threshold.
- For large, the s76 bowl and the s96 sheep are also found by "small object". The s71 dinosaur is also found by
  "object on the floor".

So the "threshold" toys are prompt-fixable too, and for both models every miss but the Lego bricks and the
out-of-range card game is prompt-fixable or within a hair of the line.

| | |
|---|---|
| Harness | houndkeeper `sim/house/baselines/misses.py` (new; `run`, `diagnose`), on base commit ae84241; the placement and scorer of `place.py`, `score.py`, `table.py` unchanged ([o0E], [oR6]) |
| DimOS | fork base a7492431f with its local working-tree changes; the wrapper `dimos/perception/detection/detectors/owlv2.py` (sha256 `d618af38…bc21c`), `Owlv2Detector.query_score_rows` |
| Models | `google/owlv2-base-patch16-ensemble`, HF snapshot `cfd3195ba4ea9592eec887ded089f4c08eff231d`; `google/owlv2-large-patch14-ensemble`, HF snapshot `95e26936e865f87db17421284

findings.name: realtime-run.md
findings.title: Real-time sim run: results
findings.excerpt:
> **Why this is here:** the sim ran 3.3x faster than real time while DimOS ran on the wall clock, so the camera saw
> about 3x fewer frames a metre and every number looked better than it would on the robot. A plain account of a
> clock mismatch that flatters a simulation, and what it cost to fix (sim-house-nights [drP] holds the result).

All numbers are from the simulator, not the real house. Numbers marked (est.) are estimates.
findings.full:
> **Why this is here:** the sim ran 3.3x faster than real time while DimOS ran on the wall clock, so the camera saw
> about 3x fewer frames a metre and every number looked better than it would on the robot. A plain account of a
> clock mismatch that flatters a simulation, and what it cost to fix (sim-house-nights [drP] holds the result).

Run overnight 22–23 Sep 2026. Raw output is in `sim/runs/nights_s8/final.txt`, with the log in `sim/runs/nights_s8/run_notes.txt`.
All numbers are from the simulator, not the real house. Numbers marked (est.) are estimates.

## Why we ran it
The sim had been running about 3.3× faster than real time. Each physics loop advanced 35 ms of sim time but waited only for 5 ms of real time, and DimOS runs on the real clock. So the robot moved about 3× faster than DimOS thought, and the camera saw about 3× fewer frames per metre.
A speed setting (`DIMOS_SIM_SPEED`) was added to DimOS's sim loop. This run used real time.

## What changed compared with the earlier run
Three things changed at once, so no single difference can be pinned on sim speed alone:
1. **Sim speed:** real time (measured 0.91–0.93×), against about 3.3×.
2. **New timeline (seed 8):** a different floor, and 12 nights instead of 8.
3. **Moving furniture:** six dining chairs, a stool and a kid's chair, each tucked in, nudged a bit, or moved a lot each night. None are pick-up targets.

Unchanged: detector v2 (frozen), the navigation fixes, the sweep route and the scoring. Tuning nights 2–4, held-out nights 5–12, scored once.

## Results (held-out nights)

| | Earlier: ~3.3×, seed 7, nights 5–8 | **Real time: seed 8 with chairs, nights 5–12** |
|---|---|---|
| Items scored | 87 | 156 |
| Found | 72% | **58%** (91/156) |
| Easy / medium / hard | 86 / 74 / 54% | 66 / 54 / 42% |
| False alarms per night | ~43 | **~18** |
| Look-closer: real finds kept | 95% | 84% |
| Look-closer: false alarms removed | 29% | 53% |
| False alarms left after look-closer | ~30 a night | **~8 a night** |
| Items never properly seen | 8 | 24 |
| Flags on chairs, or on the spot a chair left | n/a | 0 of 175 false alarms |

Old detector (v1) on the same real-time nights, for reference: 47% found, ~30 false alarms a night.

## Navigation
- 49/49 waypoints every night; 0–2 failed waypoints a night, with the robot still reaching all 49.
- Stalled 0–1% of the time it was told to move. Night 12 was 6% (39 s), cause not investigated.
- A night took about 24 minutes of real time, against about 8–10 minutes at 3.3×. The robot was told to move for about 500–680 s a night (about 112–170 s at 3.3×).

## Floor model
It got steadily sharper at real time and ended much better than the 3.3× run:

| | After night 1 | After night 12 | 3.3× run, final |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fidelity to true floor | 0.24 | 0.30 | 0.12 |
| Confidently mapped patches | 33% | 49% | 10% |
| Waviness | 1.4 cm | 2.0 cm | 4.0 cm (peaked at 4.3) |
| Coverage | 72% | 76% | 80% |

This fits the idea that real time gives the camera about 3× more frames per metre.

## Reading the results
- **Fewer false alarms is the big win.** About 8 closer looks a night after look-closer, against about 30. That's the battery-budget problem shrinking a lot.
- **The drop in finds is mostly items seen only as tiny specks.** Misses where the item was detected and then dropped went from 8 to 34, mostly specks under 8 px.
  - Likely cause, not verified: some thresholds count lidar hits per cell. They were tuned at 3.3×, and real time gives about 3× more scans.
  - The lidar "stands up" layer tripled in size (~23 → ~80 m²) and probably masks floor next to items.
- **Chairs weren't flagged, but big chair moves were barely tested.** A generator bug meant only 2 big moves in 12 nights: when a big move couldn't find space, the generator re-rolled the move type instead of retrying the position.
- **Decision (user):** we are not re-tuning for sim speed. At this point it would be tuning for the simulator rather than the real robot.
  - The d
